title: Amount of fossil change between formations measures elapsed time

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Amount of fossil change between formations measures elapsed time

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because species are produced and exterminated by slow, still-acting causes, the amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations is probably a fair, though imperfect, measure of the time elapsed, and can be used to estimate the length of the blank intervals between formations.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it follows, that the amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations probably serves as a fair measure of the lapse of actual time.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIV, “Recapitulation and Conclusion”; section “Effects of its adoption on the study of Natural history”. Scope: fossil faunas and floras of successive formations

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch14-07: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.78

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Independent numerical ages and fossil assemblages allow direct calibration and out-of-sample validation. Known rate heterogeneity makes the measure imperfect, exactly as the claim allows.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For independently radiometrically dated formation pairs, quantify fossil assemblage turnover or phylogenetic change and test its relationship with elapsed time, then use held-out intervals to assess dating error. A stable monotonic calibrated relationship supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Turnover rates vary among clades and mass extinctions.

Sampling and preservation differ among formations.

Circular biostratigraphic age assignments must be excluded.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Turnover and radiometric duration are both public variables, and a positive controlled correlation is a direct test of using organic change as a clock. Occurrence databases and the numerical time scale cover the Phanerozoic well enough for a global marine test, with coarser coverage of terrestrial formations. Sampling and facies are serious confounds and are also standard covariates in this analysis, which a small team can run.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Between consecutive formations, measure faunal dissimilarity and the radiometrically dated time span, controlling for rock volume and collection effort. The claim is confirmed if organic turnover increases with elapsed time closely enough to rank the lengths of gaps, and refuted if turnover is uncorrelated with dated duration once sampling and facies are controlled.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The claim already calls the measure imperfect, so only a weak or absent correlation with radiometric duration would refute it.

A change of facies or of collecting effort can produce faunal turnover within a short span of time.

Formations are local, and 'consecutive' units on different continents are not a single global clock.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If the amount of organic change between consecutive faunas is a fair though imperfect measure of elapsed time, then across the Phanerozoic the proportion of marine animal genera present in a stage that do not continue into the next stage should increase with the radiometric duration of the stage, and this should hold after controlling for sampling intensity.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The PBDB diversity table for marine animal genera at stage resolution was downloaded for the whole Phanerozoic; for each of the 96 stages retained (two youngest dropped) turnover was computed as the share of genera present that make their last appearance in the stage, and stage duration as the difference of its PBDB/ICS boundary ages. Spearman correlation of turnover with duration, the partial Spearman correlation controlling log occurrences, and the correlation after removing the five highest-turnover stages (Stage 4, Changhsingian, Drumian, Guzhangian, Katian) were computed.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Using Paleobiology Database stage-level diversity tables for marine animal genera (occs/diversity, count=genera, time_reso=stage, Phanerozoic, marine environments), turnover T_i for each stage i = (X_bL + X_FL) / (X_bt + X_bL + X_Ft + X_FL), the fraction of genera sampled in or ranging through stage i that make their last appearance in it, and duration D_i = early age minus late age of the stage (PBDB/ICS ages). The last two stages (Pleistocene edge, where last appearances are distorted by the Recent) are excluded. Pass if (1) the Spearman correlation between T_i and D_i across stages is positive with p < 0.05, AND (2) the partial Spearman correlation controlling for log(number of occurrences in the stage) is also positive with p < 0.05, AND (3) the correlation remains positive (point estimate > 0) when the five stages with the highest turnover (mass-extinction stages) are removed, so that the relation is not carried by catastrophes alone. 'Fair though imperfect' is operationalised as rho between 0.2 and 0.9: a rho >= 0.2 that meets (1)-(3) supports; the verdict is 'mixed' if (1) holds but (2) or (3) fails, 'refutes' if (1) fails.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Refuted if turnover between consecutive stages does not increase with stage duration (Spearman rho <= 0 or p >= 0.05), which would mean faunal change carries no information about elapsed time. Mixed if the raw correlation is positive but disappears when sampling intensity is controlled or is carried entirely by the five highest-turnover stages.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: Spearman rho, stage turnover vs stage duration (Myr)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'amount of organic change in the fossils of consecutive formations' is read as the proportion of genera that fail to pass from one stage to the next (taxonomic turnover), and 'time elapsed' as the radiometrically calibrated stage duration, a measurement unavailable to Darwin. Stages, not lithostratigraphic formations, are the units because global turnover can only be computed on a correlated time scale; the claim's use (estimating blank intervals between formations) is tested indirectly through its premise that change tracks time. Marine animals are used because their stage-level record is the most complete and standardised.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Paleobiology Database occs/diversity: marine Animalia genus counts per stage (Phanerozoic), with Foote range categories

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Turnover measured on stages correlated by biostratigraphy is partly circular: stage boundaries were historically placed at faunal changes, which inflates turnover at boundaries regardless of duration; the test asks whether, given those boundaries, longer stages still show more change.

Stage-level genus ranges are affected by uneven sampling across stages; the partial correlation controls only for occurrence count, not for facies or geographic coverage.

Taxonomic turnover is a proxy for Darwin's 'amount of organic change', which he meant morphologically; a few stages with mass extinctions dominate the upper tail of turnover.

The claim's practical use (estimating blank intervals between formations) is tested only through its premise that change tracks time.
